6L93U4CpyYo.title: The Final Sermon, Part 1
6L93U4CpyYo.one_line: Walking the Prophet's farewell Hajj through Jabir's long hadith in Muslim, up to the first paragraph of the sermon on the sanctity of life.
6L93U4CpyYo.summary: First of two nights on the Prophet's Hajj as the third lens through which to experience the pilgrimage, after Adam and Eve and Ibrahim's family. He reads the long hadith of Jabir in Sahih Muslim, one of the very few long narrations that is authentic, narrated by a companion who held the Prophet's camel rein. He follows the journey step by step: nine years in Medina without Hajj, the year spent clearing Makkah of troublemakers to avoid bloodshed, the call to Hajj that emptied the countryside into Medina, Asma bint Umays giving birth at the ihram point (which sets off a long aside on today's delayed-marriage epidemic), Jabir's picture of people in every direction while the Quran descends and is practised live, the talbiyah and its variant wordings, tawaf, the prayer behind maqam Ibrahim, sa'i, the Prophet's tears on Safa twenty years after being mocked there, Suraqah's question, Ali and Fatima, and the Prophet riding past the Hums' boundary to Arafah. Throughout he presses one argument: the Prophet deliberately allowed different practices, so difference in Islam is by design, not by mistake. He then explains how 100,000 people heard the sermon through riders, why the Prophet knew it was farewell (5:3 and Abu Bakr's sobbing), and ends with the paragraph the Prophet never dropped: your blood, wealth and honour are as sacred as this day, month and land. Love of the Prophet that coexists with harming people gives his love a bad name.

outline.heading: Three lenses on Hajj
outline.gist: Hajj can be lived through Adam and Eve, through Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il, or through the Prophet. His is the closest to us and the best documented: we know where he walked and what he said, in Hajj and in his life in Makkah.

outline.heading: The long hadith of Jabir in Sahih Muslim
outline.gist: Long hadith are rarely authentic, and this is one of a handful that are. Jabir was young, always near the Prophet in his last years, one of the five leading narrators, lived into his eighties or nineties, and his students taught the teachers of the madhhab founders.

outline.heading: Once in his life, three months before his death
outline.gist: The Prophet performed Hajj only once, in year 10, and died about three months later: a farewell Hajj as well as a farewell sermon, and the largest gathering Arabia had seen outside war. A teacher of Sahih Muslim required students to memorize this hadith; he went to another teacher instead and now regrets it.

outline.heading: The mawaqit and the dua for hearts
outline.gist: In a narration with a reasonable chain, the Prophet named the places where each region enters ihram, then turned to the horizon and asked Allah to bring their hearts to him as He had for Ibrahim's call, when people came from every corner on foot and on lean mounts.

outline.heading: Muhammad al-Baqir and the scholars of the Prophet's household
outline.gist: The hadith is told by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Husayn, the Prophet's great-grandson through Fatimah. Many Muslims leave the household out of their teaching, yet these are great scholars who taught our scholars and are more ours than anyone's.

outline.heading: The blind Jabir receives him
outline.gist: Jabir, who had lost his sight, asked who each visitor was, then opened al-Baqir's shirt, laid his hand on his chest and called him nephew. He led the prayer in a cloth too small for his shoulders, having refused gifts from rulers to keep the simplicity he lived with the Prophet, then told the story the young men memorized.

outline.heading: Nine years without Hajj
outline.gist: For a Makkan, nine years without Hajj was a great deal. Quraysh barred him; Hudaybiyyah and the Umrah nearly became war. Even after the conquest he waited about a year while Makkah was cleared of hostile people, because his concern was always to avoid more bloodshed.

outline.heading: The call to Hajj empties the countryside into Medina
outline.gist: When word spread in year 10 that the Prophet intended Hajj, people dropped what was in their hands and came to Medina: no one was going to miss Hajj with him.

outline.heading: Hajj before Islam and his dawah at its seasons
outline.gist: Arabs had performed Hajj since Ibrahim, with shirk added over the centuries. Before prophethood he performed it without the idolatry, and in Makkah he used the Hajj seasons to speak to the tribes, which is how he first met the people of Medina.

outline.heading: A farewell, and the first return without swords
outline.gist: He knew this was the last time he would see the Kaaba and the haram. Every earlier return to Makkah came with a treaty, hostility or swords; this one was peaceful, and the more perceptive companions sensed his mission was ending.

outline.heading: Hajj with the Prophet as imam
outline.gist: People do Hajj following a good scholar and copying what he does; no scholar compares with doing it behind the Prophet, so everyone wanted him as their imam.

outline.heading: Asma bint Umays and how the early generations married
outline.gist: At Dhul-Hulayfah Asma bint Umays gave birth. She married and outlived several great companions and had children with them. A woman of honour and piety was rarely left unmarried, and the waiting period exists partly so suitors do not approach while she processes a death or divorce.

outline.heading: Aside: the delayed-marriage epidemic
outline.gist: Healthy, capable Muslims in their late twenties, thirties and forties sit unmarried and childless. Fertility declines after 25, 30 and 35; a man whose first child comes at 35 should be near his last. Marry young while flexible in mind and body, and do not copy a Western model with a 60 percent divorce rate and children in two houses.

outline.heading: Rulings for menstruating and postpartum women
outline.gist: Asma sent to ask what to do: a woman who is menstruating or postpartum cannot pray but can perform Hajj, so she was told to bathe, pad herself with cloth and enter ihram.

outline.heading: A sea of people at al-Bayda
outline.gist: The Prophet prayed, mounted al-Qaswa, and from the rise of al-Bayda Jabir, who held his camel's rein, saw nothing but people on foot and riding ahead, right, left and behind.

outline.heading: The Quran descending and practised live
outline.gist: Jabir paints the moment: the Prophet among them, the Quran coming down on him, he explaining and practising it and everyone practising with him, with no war and no one upset; the happiest moment of his life, one the sheikh wishes he could stand inside.

outline.heading: Labbayk: I am coming, gladly
outline.gist: The talbiyah is a child's answer to a loved parent's call: I am on my way, happily, whatever you want. Saying it is responding to Allah's call as if coming home.

outline.heading: Variant talbiyahs: difference by design
outline.gist: People used three or four different wordings and the Prophet changed none of them while keeping his own. Room for different practice is by design, not by mistake, like the cow of Bani Israil, where any cow would have done; who claims more taqwa than the companions who were there?

outline.heading: A river with lanes, within set parameters
outline.gist: People get uptight over things that by design will be understood differently. Islam is not a line but a river with lanes: choose one and let others choose theirs. The Prophet set the essentials of Hajj, place, day and required rites, and left room in the rest.

outline.heading: Umrah inside Hajj: the three types
outline.gist: The Arabs never combined Umrah with the Hajj season. Jurists describe three types of Hajj; he assumes, despite scholarly debate, that the Prophet performed qiran, both together, which requires a sacrificial animal.

outline.heading: Tawaf and the prayer behind the maqam
outline.gist: He went straight to the black stone, jogged three circuits with the right shoulder bare and walked four, then recited 2:125 and prayed two rak'ahs with the maqam between him and the Kaaba.

outline.heading: Today: pray anywhere in the haram
outline.gist: Pilgrims today cannot copy it to the detail; pray anywhere with the intention, since Ibrahim stood throughout the area, rather than fight the crowd at the maqam and hurt yourself and others.

outline.heading: On Safa: we begin with what Allah began with
outline.gist: He returned to the stone, then climbed Safa reciting 2:158 and saying he would start where Allah started. He faced the Kaaba, which construction now hides, and said the takbir and tahlil that became the Eid takbirat.

outline.heading: Tears on Safa, twenty years later
outline.gist: Another narration describes the companions gathered at his feet saying amin to every dua while his tears ran. Twenty years earlier he stood on the same mount, was cursed by his own uncle, mocked and nearly killed. Remember both moments when you stand there: that is why you walk back and forth, because change takes time.

outline.heading: Seven lengths of sa'i
outline.gist: He walked down into the valley, quickened his pace between what are now the green lights, slowed on the climb, repeated the same dua on Marwah, and finished his seventh length there.

outline.heading: Had I known, I would have made it an Umrah
outline.gist: At Marwah he said that had he known beforehand he would not have brought the sacrificial animals and would have made it an Umrah; whoever had no animal should leave ihram and make it one.

outline.heading: Suraqah's question: forever
outline.gist: Suraqah ibn Malik, who once hunted the Prophet during the Hijrah, asked whether this was for that year only; interlacing his fingers, the Prophet said Umrah has entered Hajj forever, which is why groups today perform Hajj differently.

outline.heading: Ali and Fatima
outline.gist: Ali came from Yemen with the sacrificial animals, found Fatima out of ihram in dyed clothes and kohl, and went to 'tattletale'. The Prophet said she was right; Ali, who had tied his intention to the Prophet's, stayed in ihram.

outline.heading: Two groups, both with his permission
outline.gist: He said 'take your rituals from me', yet allowed two groups to do different things during his own Hajj.

outline.heading: Tarwiyah in Mina and a tent at Namirah
outline.gist: On the 8th the pilgrims entered ihram and went to Mina, where he prayed the day and night; after sunrise on the 9th he ordered a tent pitched at Namirah. He walks through the map of Mina, Muzdalifah and Arafah.

outline.heading: Ending the Hums
outline.gist: Quraysh called themselves the Hums, the strict ones, and never left the sacred boundary during Hajj, stopping at the Mash'ar al-Haram. The Prophet rode past it to Arafah: you are like everyone else. At midday he reached the valley and delivered his farewell sermon.

outline.heading: Delivered at least three times
outline.gist: Imam Ahmad notes he gave the sermon at least three times, never whole, choosing paragraphs on Arafah, on the day of sacrifice and the days after. In university the sheikh compiled every authentic paragraph and handed it out until a child tore the pages.

outline.heading: Two riders carry his words to 100,000
outline.gist: With no microphones, two riders known for good memories galloped his words into the crowd and returned for the next, so a two-minute text took hours. It was his last public address to his followers; listen to it at least once a year.

outline.heading: The verse of completion on Arafah (5:3)
outline.gist: Jewish men told Umar that a verse like 'today I have completed your religion' would be a yearly festival for them; Umar said he was beside the Prophet on Arafah when it came down. Later verses added no new laws.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr sobs: after the peak, the descent
outline.gist: When the Prophet recited it, Abu Bakr sobbed, knowing he would soon lose the one he loved most: after completion the graph goes down. This Hajj was the pinnacle of the whole seerah.

outline.heading: Teach the sermon like the Quran
outline.gist: Children should grow up knowing what he said in it as they know the Quran. He has gathered the authentic paragraphs into eight to ten.

outline.heading: I may not meet you after this year
outline.gist: The sermon opens: listen and understand, for I do not know whether I will meet you again after this year; Abu Bakr's crying rose higher.

outline.heading: Mu'adh sent to Yemen
outline.gist: Sending the young Mu'adh as judge and teacher, he told him he might come back to find his grave, and that those closest to him are the pious wherever they are. Mu'adh wept and, in some narrations, walked backwards to keep him in sight while the Prophet stood smiling; he returned after the Prophet's death.

outline.heading: The silence of 100,000
outline.gist: Perhaps one percent of Arabia stood before him, a number never gathered outside war. After those words there was silence except a crying baby or an animal.

outline.heading: What day, month and land is this?
outline.gist: In the paragraph he never dropped, he asked three times each, the Arab way of saying 'think again', until they thought he would rename them: it is a sacred day, a sacred month, a sacred land.

outline.heading: Your blood, wealth and honour are sacred
outline.gist: The sanctity of your lives, wealth and integrity towards one another equals the sanctity of this day, in this month, in this land, until you meet your Lord.

outline.heading: The person beside you is as sacred as all of it
outline.gist: Layer upon layer of holiness: Arafah, Dhul-Hijjah, the sacred land, the holiest of people saying the holiest words. The life, wealth and honour of the person beside you equal all of it, if not more.

outline.heading: Sanctity within the family and over wealth
outline.gist: Not even a father against his son or a child against a parent: families grow loose, taking and saying things without asking. No one's wealth is lawful to another unless given with a glad heart.

outline.heading: Have I conveyed? O Allah, be witness
outline.gist: The riders repeated it, the crowd answered yes, and he called Allah to witness, so that when people later harm and disrespect one another it will not be for lack of his telling them: a person's life, wealth and honour are a red line.

outline.heading: Don't claim to love him while harming people
outline.gist: Amid all that beauty he pointed to the ordinary person beside you. Whoever cuts everyone off in traffic, cheats those he does business with and acts as if he matters more should not claim to love the Prophet; it gives his love a bad name.

outline.heading: His one chance, and he began with this
outline.gist: With no recordings, this was the only time he would address all his followers, a hundred thousand where twenty years earlier he had six or seven. He chose his words from the essence of his character and began with sanctity; Muslims cannot afford to move beyond it.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Seerah events and their lessons
themes.note: The Prophet's farewell Hajj retold through Jabir's hadith: the years of being barred from Makkah, the patient clearing of the city, the first peaceful return, and the final public address of his life.

themes.label: Hajj, Umrah and Arafah
themes.note: Each rite is explained from the Prophet's own practice with practical advice for today's pilgrim: pray anywhere in the haram with intention, do not fight the crowd at the maqam, follow your group's type of Hajj, remember who stood on Safa.

themes.label: Jurisprudence rulings and how to approach fiqh
themes.note: Variant talbiyahs, three types of Hajj, and two groups in and out of ihram with the Prophet's permission show that legitimate difference is built into Islam by design; Islam is a river with lanes, not a line, and people get uptight over things that do not require it.

themes.label: Jurisprudence rulings and how to approach fiqh
themes.note: Suraqah's 'forever' answer and the Ali-Fatima episode: the Prophet said take your rituals from me yet let others act differently from him within the parameters.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Jabir: young, always present, one of the top five narrators, blind and poor in old age, refusing gifts to stay as simple as he was with the Prophet; the Prophet's descendants as scholars who taught the madhhab founders and are 'more ours than anyone's'.

themes.label: Marriage and the relationship between spouses
themes.note: Asma bint Umays's remarriages after each husband's death show how differently the early generations approached marriage. He calls today's unmarried, childless Muslims in their prime an epidemic that must be fixed, cites fertility medicine, and rejects the Western model of serial divorce and children in two houses.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: His thought process was always to avoid more bloodshed, so he waited a year after the conquest before bringing people to Hajj.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: On Safa, twenty years after being mocked and cursed there, he stands with the companions at his feet and tears on his face: a moment of humility and a gift from Allah to him and through him to us.

themes.label: Love: of Allah, the Prophet, and one another
themes.note: Jabir's sentimental love for anything connected to the Prophet, and the sheikh's own longing to stand among them for a moment; labbayk as a child's glad answer to a parent's call.

themes.label: Mortality, death and preparing for it
themes.note: The Prophet read 5:3 as his completion and prepared his people: Abu Bakr wept, Mu'adh was told he would find a grave, and the sermon opened with 'I may not meet you after this year'.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: By riding past the boundary where Quraysh's self-styled 'strict ones' always stopped, the Prophet ended their claim to be more religious than everyone else.

themes.label: The unlawfulness of harm and protecting others
themes.note: The one paragraph the Prophet repeated every time: a person's life, wealth and honour are as sacred as Arafah, Dhul-Hijjah and Makkah combined, even between parent and child, and wealth may only be taken with a glad heart. Claiming to love the Prophet while harming people gives his love a bad name.

themes.label: Family: parents, relatives, kinship ties
themes.note: Not even a father against his son: we get loose with family, taking and saying things without asking, forgetting that relatives are as sacred as strangers.

themes.label: Seeking knowledge, learning and scholars
themes.note: Long hadith are rarely authentic; this one is, and its narrator's students shaped the schools of law. He recalls refusing a teacher's condition to memorize it and regretting it now.

quran.point: Allah told Ibrahim to call to Hajj and people would come from every corner on foot and on lean mounts; the Prophet asks Allah to bring hearts to him the same way.
The cow of Bani Israil: any cow would have worked; they made it hard on themselves. Used to argue that room in practice is by design.
The Prophet recited 'take the standing place of Ibrahim as a place of prayer' before praying two rak'ahs behind the maqam.
'Safa and Marwah are among the rituals of Allah'; he began sa'i with Safa because Allah mentioned it first.
Remembering Allah at the Mash'ar al-Haram on leaving Arafah; cited to locate the boundary where the Hums used to stop.
'Today I have completed your religion for you' came down on Arafah during this Hajj; the Jew's remark to Umar and Abu Bakr's sobbing show it was understood as the peak and the farewell.

hadith.gist: The long hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah describing the Prophet's Hajj from Medina to its end; the frame for both nights.

Before Hajj the Prophet named the places where pilgrims enter ihram, then turned to the horizon and asked Allah to bring their hearts to him as He did for Ibrahim; narrated outside Muslim with a reasonable chain.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Husayn visited the blind Jabir, who felt for his chest, welcomed him as his nephew, led the prayer in a cloth too small for his shoulders, and then told the story of the Prophet's Hajj.
Asma bint Umays gave birth at Dhul-Hulayfah and sent to ask what to do; she was told to bathe, pad herself with cloth and enter ihram.
Jabir: I looked ahead, right, left and behind and saw only people on foot and riding; the Prophet was among us, the Quran descending on him, he knew its meaning, and whatever he did we did.
The Prophet said the talbiyah in his wording; people added other wordings and he did not object to any of them.

He touched the black stone, jogged three circuits and walked four, prayed behind maqam Ibrahim after reciting the verse, returned to the stone, then went out to Safa reciting 'Safa and Marwah are among the rituals of Allah' and saying 'we begin with what Allah began with'.
A narration that on Safa, as he made takbir and dua with the companions gathered at his feet saying amin, tears ran down his face.

At Marwah he said: had I known beforehand what I know now I would not have brought the sacrificial animals and would have made it an Umrah; whoever has no animal should exit ihram and make it an Umrah.
Suraqah ibn Malik asked whether this applied to that year only or forever; the Prophet interlaced his fingers and said Umrah has entered into Hajj forever and ever.

Ali returned from Yemen with the animals, found Fatima out of ihram in dyed clothes and kohl, and complained to the Prophet, who said she was right and asked Ali what intention he had made; since Ali had tied it to the Prophet's, he was to stay in ihram.
'Take your rituals from me', cited alongside the fact that he allowed two groups to do different things.

On the 8th they went to Mina and he prayed there; on the 9th, after sunrise, he ordered a tent at Namirah and rode on; Quraysh were sure he would stop at the Mash'ar al-Haram as they did in Jahiliyyah, but he passed on to Arafah.

A Jew said to Umar that if the verse of completion had come to them they would have made its day a festival; Umar said he knew the day and place it was revealed: on Arafah, a Friday, with the Prophet.
The sermon's opening: O people, listen and understand, for I do not know whether I will meet you after this year in this place.

Sending Mu'adh to Yemen, the Prophet said he might pass by his masjid and grave on return; Mu'adh wept, and the Prophet reassured him that those nearest to him are the pious whoever and wherever they are.

What day is this? What month? What land? asked three times each until they thought he would rename them; then: your blood, wealth and honour are as sacred to one another as this day, month and land, until you meet your Lord.
No father may transgress against his son nor son against his father; no one's wealth is lawful to another except what he gives with a glad heart.
Have I conveyed? The riders repeated his words and the people affirmed; he said, O Allah, be my witness.

maxims: By design, not by mistake
Islam is not a line; it is a river with lanes
Choose a lane and let others do something similar
The person beside you is just as sacred, if not more
Don't act like you love him if you harm people
What happens after the peak?

stories.who: The sheikh as a student of Sahih Muslim
stories.point: He refused a teacher's condition to memorize Jabir's hadith and found another teacher; he regrets it now that he no longer could.

stories.who: Muhammad al-Baqir visiting the blind Jabir
stories.point: Jabir's longing for contact with the Prophet's family, and his chosen poverty, show what love of the Prophet looked like in old age.

stories.who: Asma bint Umays
stories.point: She married and buried several of the greatest companions; the early generations did not leave capable people unmarried.

stories.who: Jabir at al-Bayda
stories.point: People in every direction, the Quran coming down, everyone practising with the Prophet: the happiest moment of his life, with no war and no one upset.

stories.who: The Prophet on Safa, year 3 of prophethood and twenty years later
stories.point: Where his own uncle cursed him before a crowd that would not listen, he now stands with the companions saying amin to his dua: patience in dawah is rewarded in time, which is why we walk back and forth.

stories.who: Suraqah ibn Malik
stories.point: The man who hunted the Prophet on the Hijrah now follows him in Hajj and asks the question that fixed the ruling for all later generations.

stories.who: Ali and Fatima
stories.point: Ali 'tattled' on Fatima for leaving ihram; the Prophet sided with her, and the two groups show flexibility granted at the source.

stories.who: The Hums of Quraysh
stories.point: Makkah's self-declared strict ones never crossed the sacred boundary; the Prophet rode past it and buried the claim that they were more religious than others.

stories.who: The sheikh's compiled sermon papers
stories.point: He assembled every authentic paragraph in university and used to hand it out until a child tore it; the sermon should be taught to children like the Quran.

stories.who: The Jew's remark to Umar and Abu Bakr's sobbing
stories.point: The companions understood 5:3 as completion, and completion meant the Prophet's time was ending.

stories.who: Mu'adh ibn Jabal sent to Yemen
stories.point: Told he might return to find a grave, he walked backwards to keep the Prophet in sight while the Prophet smiled at him; closeness to the Prophet is by piety, not blood.

stories.who: The silent crowd of 100,000
stories.point: After 'I may not meet you next year' nothing was heard but a baby or an animal; roughly one percent of Arabia listening to his last public words.

contemporary: An 'epidemic' of healthy, capable Muslims in their late 20s, 30s and 40s unmarried and childless; medical literature on fertility after 25, 30 and 35; fathers who have their first child at 35; the Western model's 60 percent divorce rate and children living in two houses
Modern Hajj packages where you follow whatever your group does and the type of Hajj depends on how deluxe the package is
Construction in Makkah means you can no longer see the Kaaba from Safa; most residents of Makkah now live outside the sacred boundary
The Eid takbirat come from what the Prophet said on Safa
Everything is online today, whereas the Prophet had one chance to address all his followers without microphones
Muslims who profess love of the Prophet yet drive aggressively and cheat everyone they do business with
A proposal that the Farewell Sermon be taught in schools alongside the Quran
takeaways: Learn the Prophet's Hajj from Jabir's hadith and perform your own rites remembering where and why he did each one, without harming others in the crowd
Accept that variant practices in Hajj and elsewhere are by design; pick a lane and stop getting uptight about things that do not require it
Marry and have children in your twenties while you are flexible in body and mind; the community must reverse the delayed-marriage trend
Treat the life, wealth and honour of the ordinary person beside you, including your own family, as more sacred than the holiest day, month and place
Do not claim love of the Prophet while cutting people off, cheating in business or acting as if your needs outrank everyone else's
Listen to or read the Farewell Sermon at least once a year at Hajj time

21:83.ar: ۞وَأَيُّوبَ إِذۡ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥٓ أَنِّي مَسَّنِيَ ٱلضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
21:83.en: And Job, when he cried unto his Lord, (saying): Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy

38:44.ar: وَخُذۡ بِيَدِكَ ضِغۡثࣰ ا فَٱضۡرِب بِّهِۦ وَلَا تَحۡنَثۡۗ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَٰهُ صَابِرࣰ اۚ نِّعۡمَ ٱلۡعَبۡدُ إِنَّهُۥٓ أَوَّابࣱ‏
38:44.en: And (it was said unto him): Take in thine hand a branch and smite therewith, and break not thine oath. Lo! We found him steadfast, how excellent a slave! Lo! he was ever turning in repentance (to his Lord)

9:119.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
9:119.en: O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful

57:27.ar: ثُمَّ قَفَّيۡنَا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم بِرُسُلِنَا وَقَفَّيۡنَا بِعِيسَى ٱبۡنِ مَرۡيَمَ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ ٱلۡإِنجِيلَۖ وَجَعَلۡنَا فِي قُلُوبِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ رَأۡفَةࣰ وَرَحۡمَةࣰۚ وَرَهۡبَانِيَّةً ٱبۡتَدَعُوهَا مَا كَتَبۡنَٰهَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ إِلَّا ٱبۡتِغَآءَ رِضۡوَٰنِ ٱللَّهِ فَمَا رَعَوۡهَا حَقَّ رِعَايَتِهَاۖ فَـَٔاتَيۡنَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مِنۡهُمۡ أَجۡرَهُمۡۖ وَكَثِيرࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ فَٰسِقُونَ
57:27.en: Then We caused Our messengers to follow in their footsteps; and We caused Jesus, son of Mary, to follow, and gave him the Gospel, and placed compassion and mercy in the hearts of those who followed him. But monasticism they invented - We ordained it not for them - only seeking Allah's pleasure, and they observed it not with right observance. So We give those of them who believe their reward, but many of them are evil-livers

wPyQLw_eEFM.one_line: Self-honesty through life's milestones, the examples of the Prophet, Ayyub and Ka'b ibn Malik, and why honest striving needs balance.
wPyQLw_eEFM.summary: He likens honesty to an ointment that stings on a burn but heals, while self-deception soothes like water until the limb is lost. The third method of self-honesty is to walk through your life's milestones, the moments of testing that arrive without dramatic music, noticing what you have selectively forgotten and why. Facing that clutter is what lets a person be comfortable in his own company, unlike those who flee solitude into drink, drugs and screens. The Prophet, despite orphanhood and poverty, was at peace with himself, could spend weeks alone in reflection, understood people without idolising or dismissing them, and showed disappointment only to help others see their own faults. Ayyub, stripped of everything, was too honest about his long years of blessing to ask for relief, saying only that harm had touched him and Allah is the Most Merciful. Ka'b ibn Malik, a poet skilled at crafting narratives, refused to invent an excuse for missing Tabuk and accepted fifty days of boycott and a tempting offer from a foreign king. Self-honesty means being a detective who suspects everything and welcomes feedback as a gift. But honesty also reveals how far one is from the ideal, which can provoke excess, so the Prophet constantly brought companions like Abu al-Darda, Abdullah ibn Amr and Hanzalah back to balance; this, he argues, is what bid'ah truly guards against.

outline.heading: Honesty is an ointment on a burn
outline.gist: It stings but heals; self-deception soothes like water until the limb must be amputated.

outline.heading: Third method: walk through your milestones
outline.gist: Most of life runs on autopilot; a few defining highs and lows are where Allah watches closely.

outline.heading: Defining moments come without music
outline.gist: Unlike films, life gives no signal; self-honesty helps you recognise testing moments past, present and future.

outline.heading: Selective forgetting
outline.gist: Combing your timeline takes a week and uncovers chapters the mind set aside; ask why.

outline.heading: Write your own biography
outline.gist: Detail the tests you passed and failed; even all failures can be redeemed by a true tawbah.

outline.heading: Do it yourself
outline.gist: Start around age ten, year by year; you can do for free what a therapist would charge for.

outline.heading: Why you avoid parts of your life
outline.gist: The answers are gold; covering clutter with a blanket works until the room has no space left.

outline.heading: Unresolved issues ruin intimate company
outline.gist: Friends and spouses with unresolved issues cannot enjoy time alone together; the same is true with yourself.

outline.heading: Fleeing yourself into distraction
outline.gist: Drink, drugs and television ease the discomfort of being left with oneself.

outline.heading: The Prophet was at ease with himself
outline.gist: Spending weeks alone in reflection at forty is only possible for one with inner peace.

outline.heading: Peace despite childhood hardship
outline.gist: Orphaned, unschooled and working as a shepherd, he still grew up with clarity and honesty about himself.

outline.heading: Know yourself to understand others
outline.gist: Without self-knowledge people either idolise or cancel others; do not try to please the masses.

outline.heading: The Prophet's disappointment as teaching
outline.gist: His smile of displeasure aimed to make people disappointed in themselves so they would learn.

outline.heading: Ayyub too honest to ask for ease
outline.gist: He was embarrassed to ask for relief until his years of hardship matched his decades of blessing.

outline.heading: Ayyub's dua without a request
outline.gist: After his wife sold her hair to feed him, he said only that harm had touched him and Allah is the Most Merciful.

outline.heading: He never asked for anything back
outline.gist: Allah restored all he lost, yet he never requested it; he saw asking to remove a trial as objecting to it.

outline.heading: Ka'b ibn Malik delays and misses Tabuk
outline.gist: He told the story himself in a long narration; meaning to follow the army, he put it off until too late.

outline.heading: The urge to construct a narrative
outline.gist: Seeing only the disabled and hypocrites left in Madinah, he faced the human pull to justify himself, though he was a poet by trade.

outline.heading: Watching others lie and succeed
outline.gist: Those ahead of him gave false excuses, received the Prophet's prayer and left unshamed, and he nearly caved.

outline.heading: Ka'b tells the truth
outline.gist: He admitted he could argue his way out with anyone but had no excuse, and the Prophet said this one has spoken truly.

outline.heading: Two slaps in a row
outline.gist: Self-honesty hurts once in facing the truth and again in bearing the consequences: fifty days of boycott.

outline.heading: Nearly recanting under pressure
outline.gist: People urged him to retract and offer an excuse; a famous man risks more by being honest.

outline.heading: The foreign king's letter
outline.gist: A northern king invited him over with a royal letter; recognising a test, he burnt it.

outline.heading: Be a detective who suspects everything
outline.gist: Like a good detective, suspect even your own beliefs and deeds to find the lies in your narrative.

outline.heading: Feedback becomes a gift
outline.gist: One searching for the truth thanks those who point out his flaws; offence comes from caring about the facade.

outline.heading: Neither true nor false feedback can hurt you
outline.gist: True criticism is useful information; false criticism cannot touch someone who knows himself.

outline.heading: Abu al-Darda and Salman
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda's devotion led him to neglect his wife; Salman corrected him and the Prophet confirmed that body, soul and family have rights.

outline.heading: The three who vowed extreme worship
outline.gist: The Prophet told them his sunnah of praying and sleeping, fasting and eating, and marrying was the model.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Amr and the Quran
outline.gist: He bargained down to completing it every three days and later regretted not keeping the Prophet's easier advice.

outline.heading: Hanzalah fears hypocrisy
outline.gist: Feeling spiritual heights with the Prophet and ordinary life at home, he was told there is an hour for this and an hour for that.

outline.heading: The Prophet's job was bringing people back
outline.gist: He moderated honest people's excess; today scholars beg people just to pray.

outline.heading: What bid'ah really guards against
outline.gist: It names exaggerated responses that destroy functionality, like monastic celibacy; the Prophet always kept his roles and simple joys.

outline.heading: Strive to resemble him, not exceed him
outline.gist: Honesty shows Jannah is beyond any price, but the answer is to follow the Prophet closely, not to do more.

outline.heading: An honest community needs regulators, not beggars
outline.gist: Begging people to give time and wealth cheapens the call; leaders should only need to keep people from going overboard.

22:27.ar: وَأَذِّن فِي ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡحَجِّ يَأۡتُوكَ رِجَالࣰ ا وَعَلَىٰ كُلِّ ضَامِرࣲ يَأۡتِينَ مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقࣲ‏
22:27.en: And proclaim unto mankind the pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine

22:28.ar: لِّيَشۡهَدُواْ مَنَٰفِعَ لَهُمۡ وَيَذۡكُرُواْ ٱسۡمَ ٱللَّهِ فِيٓ أَيَّامࣲ مَّعۡلُومَٰتٍ عَلَىٰ مَا رَزَقَهُم مِّنۢ بَهِيمَةِ ٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِۖ فَكُلُواْ مِنۡهَا وَأَطۡعِمُواْ ٱلۡبَآئِسَ ٱلۡفَقِيرَ
22:28.en: That they may witness things that are of benefit to them, and mention the name of Allah on appointed days over the beast of cattle that He hath bestowed upon them. Then eat thereof and feed therewith the poor unfortunate

7:23.ar: قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمۡنَآ أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمۡ تَغۡفِرۡ لَنَا وَتَرۡحَمۡنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡخَٰسِرِينَ
7:23.en: They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost

7:172.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِنۢ بَنِيٓ ءَادَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمۡ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمۡ وَأَشۡهَدَهُمۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمۡ أَلَسۡتُ بِرَبِّكُمۡۖ قَالُواْ بَلَىٰ شَهِدۡنَآۚ أَن تَقُولُواْ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ إِنَّا كُنَّا عَنۡ هَٰذَا غَٰفِلِينَ
7:172.en: And (remember) when thy Lord brought forth from the Children of Adam, from their reins, their seed, and made them testify of themselves, (saying): Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify. (That was) lest ye should say at the Day of Resurrection: Lo! of this we were unaware

38:26.ar: يَٰدَاوُۥدُ إِنَّا جَعَلۡنَٰكَ خَلِيفَةࣰ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ فَٱحۡكُم بَيۡنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَلَا تَتَّبِعِ ٱلۡهَوَىٰ فَيُضِلَّكَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَضِلُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ لَهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدُۢ بِمَا نَسُواْ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡحِسَابِ
38:26.en: (And it was said unto him): O David! Lo! We have set thee as a viceroy in the earth; therefor judge aright between mankind, and follow not desire that it beguile thee from the way of Allah. Lo! those who wander from the way of Allah have an awful doom, forasmuch as they forgot the Day of Reckoning

71:28.ar: رَّبِّ ٱغۡفِرۡ لِي وَلِوَٰلِدَيَّ وَلِمَن دَخَلَ بَيۡتِيَ مُؤۡمِنࣰ ا وَلِلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتِۖ وَلَا تَزِدِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ إِلَّا تَبَارَۢا
71:28.en: My Lord! Forgive me and my parents and him who entereth my house believing, and believing men and believing women, and increase not the wrong-doers in aught save ruin

14:37.en: Our Lord! Lo! I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House, our Lord! that they may establish proper worship; so incline some hearts of men that they may yearn toward them, and provide Thou them with fruits in order that they may be thankful

20:118.ar: إِنَّ لَكَ أَلَّا تَجُوعَ فِيهَا وَلَا تَعۡرَىٰ
20:118.en: It is (vouchsafed) unto thee that thou hungerest not therein nor art naked

20:119.ar: وَأَنَّكَ لَا تَظۡمَؤُاْ فِيهَا وَلَا تَضۡحَىٰ
20:119.en: And that thou thirstest not therein nor art exposed to the sun's heat

20:120.ar: فَوَسۡوَسَ إِلَيۡهِ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ قَالَ يَٰٓـَٔادَمُ هَلۡ أَدُلُّكَ عَلَىٰ شَجَرَةِ ٱلۡخُلۡدِ وَمُلۡكࣲ لَّا يَبۡلَىٰ
20:120.en: But the devil whispered to him, saying: O Adam! Shall I show thee the tree of immortality and power that wasteth not away

2:30.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ خَلِيفَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَجۡعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفۡسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسۡفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ وَنَحۡنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَۖ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
2:30.en: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not

2:31.ar: وَعَلَّمَ ءَادَمَ ٱلۡأَسۡمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ فَقَالَ أَنۢبِـُٔونِي بِأَسۡمَآءِ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
2:31.en: And He taught Adam all the names, then showed them to the angels, saying: Inform Me of the names of these, if ye are truthful

7:22.ar: فَدَلَّىٰهُمَا بِغُرُورࣲۚ فَلَمَّا ذَاقَا ٱلشَّجَرَةَ بَدَتۡ لَهُمَا سَوۡءَٰتُهُمَا وَطَفِقَا يَخۡصِفَانِ عَلَيۡهِمَا مِن وَرَقِ ٱلۡجَنَّةِۖ وَنَادَىٰهُمَا رَبُّهُمَآ أَلَمۡ أَنۡهَكُمَا عَن تِلۡكُمَا ٱلشَّجَرَةِ وَأَقُل لَّكُمَآ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنَ لَكُمَا عَدُوࣱّ مُّبِينࣱ‏
7:22.en: Thus did he lead them on with guile. And when they tasted of the tree their shame was manifest to them and they began to hide (by heaping) on themselves some of the leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called them, (saying): Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you: Lo! Satan is an open enemy to you

2:37.ar: فَتَلَقَّىٰٓ ءَادَمُ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ كَلِمَٰتࣲ فَتَابَ عَلَيۡهِۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
2:37.en: Then Adam received from his Lord words (of revelation), and He relented toward him. Lo! He is the relenting, the Merciful

2:260.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيۡفَ تُحۡيِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۖ قَالَ أَوَلَمۡ تُؤۡمِنۖ قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَٰكِن لِّيَطۡمَئِنَّ قَلۡبِيۖ قَالَ فَخُذۡ أَرۡبَعَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلطَّيۡرِ فَصُرۡهُنَّ إِلَيۡكَ ثُمَّ ٱجۡعَلۡ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ جَبَلࣲ مِّنۡهُنَّ جُزۡءࣰ ا ثُمَّ ٱدۡعُهُنَّ يَأۡتِينَكَ سَعۡيࣰ اۚ وَٱعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
2:260.en: And when Abraham said (unto his Lord): My Lord! Show me how Thou givest life to the dead, He said: Dost thou not believe? Abraham said: Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease. (His Lord) said: Take four of the birds and cause them to incline unto thee, then place a part of them on each hill, then call them, they will come to thee in haste, and know that Allah is Mighty, Wise

DvS9e2Z_yV4.title: The Spirituality of Hajj, Part 1
DvS9e2Z_yV4.one_line: Hajj read through three parallel stories, beginning with Adam and Eve: their fall, repentance at Arafah, planning at Muzdalifah, defeating Shaytan at Mina and building the first House.
DvS9e2Z_yV4.summary: After a week on the rulings of Hajj, the sheikh turns to its meaning: without the symbolism, the pilgrim travels across the world to walk around rocks. He proposes three parallel lines to reflect on during Hajj: Adam and Eve, Ibrahim and his family, and the Prophet and his Companions, plus the pilgrim's own. Most of the night goes to Adam and Eve. Placed in a safe garden, Adam resented being a servant who would die; Shaytan exploited his fear and greed, the two drives of the nafs. Sent down, the couple parted at Safa and Marwa and wandered for years, learning to value what they lost. They reunited at Arafah, where knowledge turned into real understanding (ma'rifah) and the first repentance occurred, and where Allah drew all their descendants out and took the covenant. Muzdalifah is drawing close and planning; Mina is resolve and hope; at al-Aqabah Adam stoned Shaytan; then he built the Ka'bah as a home for all of Allah's servants. Pilgrims stand equally as children of the same parents. He adds the tragedy of Qabil and Habil, the gift of Shith who taught the shared ethics found in every religion, and begins Ibrahim's line with Hajar left in the valley, trusting that Allah commanded it.

outline.heading: Every act of worship has an outer form and an inner meaning
outline.gist: Last week's rulings tell you what to do; without the purpose behind the movements, worship like salah feels awkward.

outline.heading: Without its meaning, Hajj is just rocks and sand
outline.gist: Leaving a green country to walk around stones makes no sense unless you understand why you are there.

outline.heading: Once in a lifetime is enough
outline.gist: Hajj understood properly changes a life; repeating it takes places from Muslims who will never get to go.

outline.heading: The Arabs knew Hajj but corrupted it
outline.gist: Ibrahim's descendants kept the rite but filled it with idolatrous practice, which the Prophet cleansed.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's call and the promise that people will come
outline.gist: People arrive on foot and on lean camels from every distant land, to witness benefits, remember Allah and feed the poor.

outline.heading: Three parallel lines of reflection
outline.gist: Adam and Eve, Ibrahim's family, and the Prophet with his Companions; keep at least one clearly in mind during Hajj.

outline.heading: Why the Adam story at Mecca was common knowledge
outline.gist: The Quran corrects common knowledge only when it is wrong; the Prophet refined rather than replaced what the Arabs knew.

outline.heading: Adam's garden was a safe place, not the final Paradise
outline.gist: He holds the view that the garden was a protected place where Adam would not hunger or be exposed, since no one is expelled from the eternal Paradise.

outline.heading: Resenting servanthood and death
outline.gist: Adam disliked being a servant who would die; Shaytan offered kingship and immortality, but servanthood to Allah means serving people and the world.

outline.heading: The angels' question and Adam's capacity to learn
outline.gist: Allah taught Adam the names and showed the angels a creature with a remarkable intellect; nature outside the garden is brutal.

outline.heading: Fear and greed: the nafs in a nutshell
outline.gist: Adam could not yet control his fear of death and his wish for more, the two drives that make people do foolish things.

outline.heading: The first sin was destined: Musa argues with Adam
outline.gist: Musa blames Adam on the Day of Judgment and Adam wins the argument; Adam was destined for earth before he was created.

outline.heading: Their weaknesses exposed
outline.gist: Their nakedness symbolised every inner weakness laid bare: greed, fear, arrogance, vanity, laziness.

outline.heading: No one has lost more than Adam
outline.gist: Taught directly by Allah and given every security, he lost it all with no way back in his lifetime.

outline.heading: Parting at Safa and Marwa
outline.gist: The stories say Adam came down on Safa and Eve on Marwa, too ashamed to speak, and walked off in different directions.

outline.heading: Years lost: learning to value blessings
outline.gist: Most people only appreciate what they had once it is gone; losing each other was worse than losing the garden.

outline.heading: Reunited at Arafah
outline.gist: Adam saw Eve from the mount and they recognised each other, the root of the name Arafah.

outline.heading: Information versus true understanding (ilm and ma'rifah)
outline.gist: Adam had been taught but did not yet understand; real comprehension came only after loss.

outline.heading: Being a servant is the best description of you
outline.gist: They grasped they must control their whims and that servanthood and stewardship are the greatest honours; losing one thing need not mean throwing away everything.

outline.heading: The first repentance in human history
outline.gist: Allah gave Adam words to say: we have wronged ourselves; owning the wrong without blaming Allah is the key, and we stand where they stood to do the same.

outline.heading: Standing at Arafah in daylight
outline.gist: The standing is in daylight because it is a time of enlightenment, and the long walk to Muzdalifah marks the gap between understanding and action.

outline.heading: The covenant of Adam's descendants
outline.gist: At Arafah Allah brought out all of Adam's children and they testified that He is their Lord.

outline.heading: The part of you that always knows its Lord
outline.gist: Beneath the noise of the nafs, everyone carries something that calls them back to Allah, so no one can claim they never knew.

outline.heading: Adam the first khalifa
outline.gist: Ibn Abbas says Adam understood his purpose as servant and steward; the first revealed use of the word khalifa was for Dawud.

outline.heading: Dawud's forty years and the fear of death
outline.gist: Adam gave Dawud forty years of his life, then nearly took them back; Islam asks us to accept death, not to enjoy it.

outline.heading: All equally children of Adam and Eve
outline.gist: Simple ihram clothing shows that no race, wealth or age gives anyone a greater claim to the parents who stood there.

outline.heading: Muzdalifah: drawing close and making a plan
outline.gist: From zulfa, nearness; the couple planned their family and their resistance to Shaytan, so pilgrims gather pebbles in preparation.

outline.heading: Why Arafah lies outside the Haram
outline.gist: An early scholar asked his teacher this before Hajj; the answer: the Haram is Allah's courtyard and Arafah His door, where servants wait until He lets them in.

outline.heading: Mina: the place of hopes and resolve
outline.gist: Every prophet performed Hajj; at Mina Adam and Eve resolved to earn their way back to the garden, while Shaytan watched his victory unravel.

outline.heading: Al-Aqabah: Adam stones Shaytan
outline.gist: Shaytan confronted Adam at the obstacle and Adam drove him off with pebbles; then came the first sacrifice.

outline.heading: Adam builds the first House
outline.gist: Commanded to build, Adam laid the Ka'bah and circled it; it was later lost and revived by Nuh and then Ibrahim.

outline.heading: Prophets who passed through these valleys
outline.gist: Seventy prophets prayed at Masjid al-Khayf, and the Prophet named valleys where he could almost see Musa and Yunus passing in pilgrimage.

outline.heading: Bayt means home and family
outline.gist: Allah needs no house; we do. Nuh's prayer for whoever enters his house means his family; the Ka'bah is a home for all of Allah's servants.

outline.heading: Why we face the House in every prayer
outline.gist: Each takbir toward the Ka'bah keeps alive the story of when our parents understood their purpose.

outline.heading: Your own line: what will you realise and change?
outline.gist: Beyond reflecting on humanity as one family, ask what you will understand at Arafah, plan at Muzdalifah and throw away at Mina.

outline.heading: Mecca's beauty is history, not scenery
outline.gist: Like children fighting over an ugly family house, the value is sentimental: this is where our parents began the story.

outline.heading: The Ka'bah as the first family home
outline.gist: Building a bayt made them a family; Hajj celebrates humanity under Allah's care and the value of figuring things out for yourself.

outline.heading: Qabil, Habil and the gift of Shith
outline.gist: Stories place the murder of Habil near Mina, the worst grief of Adam and Eve, followed by the glad news of Shith, given fifty scriptures.

outline.heading: Shared ethics in every religion
outline.gist: All faiths teach honesty, trust and that ends do not justify means, against philosophies of playing dirty; he traces this to Shith's teaching.

outline.heading: Adam's death at Abu Qubays
outline.gist: Adam died at the foot of Abu Qubays by Safa, at peace that Shith had inherited his realisations; the place of the graves is uncertain.

outline.heading: Summing up the line of Adam and Eve
outline.gist: Hajj is returning to the place where our parents learned, repented and built the first home.

outline.heading: The lines progress from two people to the whole ummah
outline.gist: Adam and Eve, then Ibrahim's family of three, then the Prophet's community; the themes of unity and repentance reveal themselves to anyone who lives them.

outline.heading: Ibrahim, Sarah and Hajar
outline.gist: Sarah's pain at Hajar's son led Ibrahim to separate them; Allah sent them much farther than he planned.

outline.heading: The journey south to a forgotten sacred place
outline.gist: Ibrahim had travelled from Iraq to Egypt but never south; the Ka'bah's site had been lost and some thought it was in Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Leaving his family in a barren valley
outline.gist: Ibrahim's prayer shows he knew the site of the Sacred House before it was rebuilt; this was the first of two partings from Isma'il.

outline.heading: Ibrahim the questioner who never questioned a command
outline.gist: He argued with his people, the king and even asked how Allah revives the dead, yet obeyed a direct command without question.

outline.heading: Hajar: is it Allah who commanded this?
outline.gist: When he nodded, she accepted that Allah would not abandon them; Ibrahim's line of Hajj begins here.

outline.heading: Outro

g-8ISIHDd_4.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Honesty, Episode 6
g-8ISIHDd_4.one_line: Truthfulness ranks just below prophethood: Abu Dharr's lesson, mistakes versus patterns, the bubble of compounding lies, and meeting Allah without argument.
g-8ISIHDd_4.summary: He opens with the verse ranking the truthful directly below the prophets and above the martyrs, noting that knowledge is absent from the list because it can lift or sink a person. A Bedouin who wanted only martyrdom was told that if he was truthful with Allah, Allah would be true to him, and he died exactly as he described. Abu Dharr, an early convert, was told plainly he was unfit to lead even two people, accepted it without resentment, and so preserved a legacy the Prophet praised for truthfulness. When reviewing your timeline, look for defining moments, learn from losses as a chess player studies defeats, and see many mistakes as proof of great potential. Ask why repeatedly to reach root causes, and attend to patterns before one-off mistakes, often a poor sleep routine. The opposite of self-honesty is ignoring the elephant, a survival skill useful outwardly but ruinous inwardly. Lies compound into a bubble that reality eventually pops, as with overprotected children, elderly cancer patients unable to accept death, or people whose faith collapses on meeting suffering they always knew existed. Many Muslims hold inherited, false beliefs such as blaming jinn or a scrap of paper for their problems. Saying 'it is only me' is empowering, and those saved on the Day come without argument, in remorse and humility. In the Q&A he discusses owning one's share of a failure, the will to change, strict traditional circles, and knowledge without the tools of tazkiyah.

outline.heading: Opening
Self-honesty is an approach to life
outline.gist: Revise and reflect on the concepts so they become habits rather than heard information.

outline.heading: The truthful rank below prophets, above martyrs
outline.gist: The verse lists prophets, the truthful, martyrs and the righteous; the siddiqin outrank even martyrs.

outline.heading: Knowledge is not on the list
outline.gist: Knowledge is a tool that can bring one closer to Allah or further away; it does not define rank.

outline.heading: The Bedouin who wanted an arrow, not booty
outline.gist: Refusing his share of spoils, he said he wanted martyrdom; the Prophet said if he was truthful Allah would grant it, and he was brought back struck where he had pointed.

outline.heading: Abu Dharr's seniority
outline.gist: One of the earliest Muslims, he could reasonably expect a position of leadership, as seniority normally brings.

outline.heading: Told he would not lead even two
outline.gist: The Prophet told him plainly he was weak at leadership, and Abu Dharr accepted it without resentment.

outline.heading: Honest words preserved his legacy
outline.gist: Given power he would have mismanaged people; because the Prophet told him the truth he is remembered as among the most truthful companions.

outline.heading: A sting now or agony later
outline.gist: Truth hurts inflated self-images at first but saves far greater pain; Abu Dharr avoided leadership all his life.

outline.heading: Look for defining moments
outline.gist: In reviewing your timeline, find the decisions, or failures to decide, that shaped what followed.

outline.heading: Learn from losses like a chess player
outline.gist: There is little to learn from successes; review the games you lost.

outline.heading: Many mistakes mean great potential
outline.gist: Finding only two mistakes means you can barely improve; finding a thousand is uplifting.

outline.heading: Ask why until you reach the root
outline.gist: Behaviour such as cowardice is usually a symptom; the root cause may drive a hundred others.

outline.heading: Patterns before one-off mistakes
outline.gist: What you do repeatedly will make or ruin you; one-time errors can wait.

outline.heading: Lifestyle patterns hide in plain sight
outline.gist: Poor grades may come from never sleeping before one; a day that starts at noon is already over.

outline.heading: Fix the basic routine first
outline.gist: Many who bring him spiritual complaints have no healthy daily routine at all.

outline.heading: The opposite: ignoring the elephant
outline.gist: Lying to yourself is acting as if the problem is not there, a skill learned in childhood.

outline.heading: Selective stupidity works outwardly, not inwardly
outline.gist: Children in war must ignore explosions and a wise leader ignores insults, but applied to yourself it is ruinous.

outline.heading: Welcome those who show you your flaws
outline.gist: Long-ignored faults become scenery; like Umar, the honest welcome anyone who gifts them their faults.

outline.heading: Lies compound into a bubble
outline.gist: One lie stands out among truths, so it must be surrounded by others, including lies about reality.

outline.heading: Overprotected children
outline.gist: Shielded from too many truths, they struggle when the bubble pops.

outline.heading: Patients in their seventies who cannot accept death
outline.gist: In oncology he sees elderly people devastated by a basic truth because they told themselves they had plenty of time.

outline.heading: Suffering does not disprove God
outline.gist: People who deny the world's brutality build a fitting image of God and then lose faith; we know Allah because of pain, not despite it.

outline.heading: The early Arabs never lost faith over pain
outline.gist: Infant deaths and desert deaths were normal to them, and no one questioned the Prophet over suffering.

outline.heading: An army of lies
outline.gist: Lies camouflage each other; only by zooming out do you see the whole structure.

outline.heading: We ask converts for honesty; what about you?
outline.gist: Non-Muslims find Islam only by admitting their lives are flawed; born Muslims must do the same.

outline.heading: Inherited beliefs that are not Islam
outline.gist: Honesty exposes cultural baggage, and most Muslims hold a distorted picture of their faith.

outline.heading: Blaming jinn and a scrap of paper
outline.gist: People blame possession or a charm left by an aunt rather than tempers, anxiety and bad choices.

outline.heading: 'It's only me' is empowering
outline.gist: If outside forces controlled you, change would be impossible; admitting your choices gives full room to grow.

outline.heading: Those saved come without argument
outline.gist: In every account of forgiveness the person offers no defence, only remorse and humility.

outline.heading: Habitual liars keep constructing stories
outline.gist: With the stakes highest, the self-deceiver will try to explain away his record.

outline.heading: Whoever argues the reckoning is punished
outline.gist: The danger is not Allah questioning you but you arguing with Him as if you had the better case.

outline.heading: The hopeless who are forgiven
outline.gist: Someone raised in crime with no role models but who comes with no excuses may find his way to forgiveness.

outline.heading: Outro
Interlude
Question: the economy or me?
outline.gist: Truth is multifaceted; of nepotism, a bad economy and your own candidacy, only your share is yours to fix.

outline.heading: Complaining in coffee shops gets you nowhere
outline.gist: Those who say they contribute nothing to their problems are like conspiracy theorists.

outline.heading: Divine decree and your contribution
outline.gist: Distinguish what Allah decrees beyond your control from what He destines you to fulfil; reliance without doing your part means nothing.

outline.heading: Medical school applicants who don't know why
outline.gist: Reapplying without identifying the weaknesses in your file is delusional thinking.

outline.heading: No one can do this for you
outline.gist: You could win any argument against him about your faults; self-honesty is a decision only you can make.

outline.heading: Question: how do I change?
outline.gist: There is no pill; once you identify a flaw, you must decide to change it.

outline.heading: A path, not a recipe
outline.gist: Ask about concepts, definitions and theory; the effort and choices are yours.

outline.heading: The will is there when you want it
outline.gist: A young man in love moves mountains, and Hajar's desperate running brought forth Zamzam; the question is whether you will apply it.

outline.heading: Question: the spiritual orders
outline.gist: Those that survived kept a sound method; all scholars prescribed practices to keep the heart alive, some systematically.

outline.heading: His struggle to move groups forward
outline.gist: He was taught a step-by-step progression but finds most attendees stay at the first step, and blames his own method.

outline.heading: The strict circles he attended
outline.gist: Those who skipped the twice-daily wird were told not to return; he was once removed, and sitting with his teacher was a privilege.

outline.heading: Question: knowledge without the tools
outline.gist: Without self-value, humility, mortality and self-honesty, knowledge leads the wrong way, as with the scholar among the first thrown into the fire.

outline.heading: Brilliant but bad people
outline.gist: Scholars and scientists can cash in on knowledge while lacking its virtues, which is why tazkiyah must be taught.

outline.heading: Character traits make learning possible
outline.gist: Without objectivity, open-mindedness, acceptance of truth, humility and compassion one cannot learn, only collect information.

outline.heading: The danger of those who know a lot
outline.gist: Knowledge gives power to manipulate, which is why the Quran pairs knowledge with what must accompany it.

2:125.en: And when We made the House (at Makka) a resort for mankind and sanctuary, (saying): Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray). And We imposed a duty upon Abraham and Ishmael, (saying): Purify My house for those who go around and those who meditate therein and those who bow down and prostrate themselves (in worship)

2:126.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ ٱجۡعَلۡ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا ءَامِنࣰ ا وَٱرۡزُقۡ أَهۡلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ مَنۡ ءَامَنَ مِنۡهُم بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِۚ قَالَ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُۥ قَلِيلࣰ ا ثُمَّ أَضۡطَرُّهُۥٓ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلنَّارِۖ وَبِئۡسَ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
2:126.en: And when Abraham prayed: My Lord! Make this a region of security and bestow upon its people fruits, such of them as believe in Allah and the Last Day, He answered: As for him who disbelieveth, I shall leave him in contentment for a while, then I shall compel him to the doom of Fire - a hapless journey's end

2:127.ar: وَإِذۡ يَرۡفَعُ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ ٱلۡقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلۡبَيۡتِ وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلۡ مِنَّآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
2:127.en: And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, (Abraham prayed): Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower

2:128.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱجۡعَلۡنَا مُسۡلِمَيۡنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةࣰ مُّسۡلِمَةࣰ لَّكَ وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا وَتُبۡ عَلَيۡنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
2:128.en: Our Lord! And make us submissive unto Thee and of our seed a nation submissive unto Thee, and show us our ways of worship, and relent toward us. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Relenting, the Merciful

2:129.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱبۡعَثۡ فِيهِمۡ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
2:129.en: Our Lord! And raise up in their midst a messenger from among them who shall recite unto them Thy revelations, and shall instruct them in the Scripture and in wisdom and shall make them grow. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Mighty, Wise

2:130.ar: وَمَن يَرۡغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ إِلَّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفۡسَهُۥۚ وَلَقَدِ ٱصۡطَفَيۡنَٰهُ فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَإِنَّهُۥ فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
2:130.en: And who forsaketh the religion of Abraham save him who befooleth himself? Verily We chose him in the world, and lo! in the Hereafter he is among the righteous

53:39.ar: وَأَن لَّيۡسَ لِلۡإِنسَٰنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ
53:39.en: And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort

2:260.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيۡفَ تُحۡيِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۖ قَالَ أَوَلَمۡ تُؤۡمِنۖ قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَٰكِن لِّيَطۡمَئِنَّ قَلۡبِيۖ قَالَ فَخُذۡ أَرۡبَعَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلطَّيۡرِ فَصُرۡهُنَّ إِلَيۡكَ ثُمَّ ٱجۡعَلۡ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ جَبَلࣲ مِّنۡهُنَّ جُزۡءࣰ ا ثُمَّ ٱدۡعُهُنَّ يَأۡتِينَكَ سَعۡيࣰ اۚ وَٱعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
2:260.en: And when Abraham said (unto his Lord): My Lord! Show me how Thou givest life to the dead, He said: Dost thou not believe? Abraham said: Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease. (His Lord) said: Take four of the birds and cause them to incline unto thee, then place a part of them on each hill, then call them, they will come to thee in haste, and know that Allah is Mighty, Wise

47:36.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا لَعِبࣱ وَلَهۡوࣱۚ وَإِن تُؤۡمِنُواْ وَتَتَّقُواْ يُؤۡتِكُمۡ أُجُورَكُمۡ وَلَا يَسۡـَٔلۡكُمۡ أَمۡوَٰلَكُمۡ
47:36.en: The life of the world is but a sport and a pastime. And if ye believe and ward off (evil). He will give you your wages, and will not ask of you your wordly wealth

47:37.ar: إِن يَسۡـَٔلۡكُمُوهَا فَيُحۡفِكُمۡ تَبۡخَلُواْ وَيُخۡرِجۡ أَضۡغَٰنَكُمۡ
47:37.en: If He should ask it of you and importune you, ye would hoard it, and He would bring to light your (secret) hates

22:27.ar: وَأَذِّن فِي ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡحَجِّ يَأۡتُوكَ رِجَالࣰ ا وَعَلَىٰ كُلِّ ضَامِرࣲ يَأۡتِينَ مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقࣲ‏
22:27.en: And proclaim unto mankind the pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine

2:132.ar: وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعۡقُوبُ يَٰبَنِيَّ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱصۡطَفَىٰ لَكُمُ ٱلدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنتُم مُّسۡلِمُونَ
2:132.en: The same did Abraham enjoin upon his sons, and also Jacob, (saying): O my sons! Lo! Allah hath chosen for you the (true) religion; therefore die not save as men who have surrendered (unto Him)

0yJtIYgnmcU.title: The Spirituality of Hajj, Part 2
0yJtIYgnmcU.one_line: The line of Ibrahim's family in Hajj: Hajar's sa'i as relentless effort, Zamzam, the sacrifice of Isma'il, stoning Shaytan's foothold, and rebuilding the Ka'bah.
0yJtIYgnmcU.summary: The second night of the Hajj series follows the line of Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il. Left in an empty valley, Hajar ran seven times between Safa and Marwa, though Jibril did not need her search to find them. The sheikh makes this the core of sa'i: a Muslim must always do his best even when it seems useless, as in the rain prayer or the hadith of planting a sapling as the Hour comes, and as the Prophet did when, rejected by twenty-six tribes, he approached six poor youths from Yathrib. Effort must carry the passion of a terrified mother, and career, family and wealth should be means to serving the deen, so losing them does not crush you. He adds that Hajar's urge to contain Zamzam shows our need for control, then tells how the Jurhum tribe settled honourably by the water. The sacrifice story is the birth of the word Muslim: Ibrahim, a lifelong questioner, obeyed without question, and Isma'il consented. Stoning the jamarat is throwing away the weaknesses through which Shaytan enters, since he has no power otherwise. Eid celebrates that Allah never commands anything against our interest. He closes with father and son rebuilding the House, tawaf in harmony with the cosmos, and Ibrahim's message from the seventh heaven.

outline.heading: Recap: the three lines of Hajj
outline.gist: After Adam and Eve, tonight follows Ibrahim's family, the line the Quran and hadith describe most.

outline.heading: Hajar left in the valley
outline.gist: Ibrahim leaves his wife and newborn in a barren valley; once she learns it is Allah's command she trusts He will not neglect them.

outline.heading: Hajar's search between Safa and Marwa
outline.gist: She climbed each hill to call for help and jogged where she lost sight of her son, which is why pilgrims jog between the green lights.

outline.heading: The seventh run and the gift of Zamzam
outline.gist: On the seventh time she heard a sound and found Jibril with Isma'il striking the earth; sa'i, a pillar of Hajj, follows a woman's footsteps.

outline.heading: Sa'i means striving: you get what you worked for
outline.gist: A person receives what he strove for even if he never achieved it; her running achieved nothing practical, yet the story was arranged so she would try.

outline.heading: Always act, even when nothing is in your control
outline.gist: Even in drought Muslims go out for the rain prayer: there is never a situation in which sitting idle is allowed.

outline.heading: Calculating her best and leaving the rest to Allah
outline.gist: Hajar worked out the most effective search; before Allah the charge that you did not try your best has no answer.

outline.heading: Plant the sapling even as the Hour comes
outline.gist: The famous hadith shows your job is never to weigh the outcome, only to take the best step available.

outline.heading: The Prophet and six youths at Mina
outline.gist: Rejected by some twenty-six tribes, he stayed until the last day and spoke to six poor young men from Yathrib, the beginning of the hijrah story.

outline.heading: The same mentality as Hajar
outline.gist: His persistence came from the lesson of sa'i: you are held to how hard you tried, not what you achieved.

outline.heading: Career and family as means, Islam as the cause
outline.gist: Make the deen your central cause and everything else a means; then losses do not devastate you, and the outcome of Islam is not yours to control.

outline.heading: Effort with the passion of a frightened mother
outline.gist: No emotion surpasses a young mother afraid for her newborn; work for the deen must carry that passion, which men can hardly grasp.

outline.heading: Never stay down: the relentless Prophet
outline.gist: Winners keep getting up; the Prophet wore out his opponents by never giving up until they finally listened.

outline.heading: Seven as a symbol of endless repetition
outline.gist: In Arabic seven and seventy signify repeating without end, which is why sa'i is seven lengths.

outline.heading: Hajar contains Zamzam: our need for control
outline.gist: The Prophet said Zamzam would have been a flowing spring had she left it; we struggle to accept we control almost nothing.

outline.heading: The Jurhum tribe settles by the water
outline.gist: A Yemeni tribe displaced by a broken dam saw birds circling, honourably asked Hajar's permission and paid her for the water.

outline.heading: Zamzam: a spring in the middle of the desert
outline.gist: He visited the pumps where his father worked; raw Zamzam has a unique scent and taste, and what is served today is mixed.

outline.heading: Drinking Zamzam with dua
outline.gist: It is sunnah to drink and make dua as Hajar did; Allah answered her by sending a tribe with ethics.

outline.heading: Isma'il grows up speaking Arabic
outline.gist: Raised among the eloquent Jurhum, he spoke Arabic and not his father's language, so Hajar had to translate between them.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's prayer accepted
outline.gist: His dua for them to keep prayer, for hearts to incline to them and for provision was answered.

outline.heading: The vision of sacrifice and the day of reflection
outline.gist: Prophets' dreams are revelation but not decisive, so Ibrahim waited; the vision returned until the day of sacrifice, and he consulted his son.

outline.heading: A questioning prophet who did not question
outline.gist: Isma'il was old enough to consent; Ibrahim, who questioned everything, asked nothing when commanded: the heart of the Eid story.

outline.heading: When the son reached the age of striving
outline.gist: The command came exactly when Isma'il could finally work alongside his father.

outline.heading: The day the word Muslim was born
outline.gist: When both submitted their wills to Allah, the description Muslim came into being; the place lies just past the jamarat.

outline.heading: Shaytan tempts Hajar, Isma'il and Ibrahim
outline.gist: On the walk Shaytan whispered to each of them in turn and each drove him away with stones.

outline.heading: Relate to one of the three
outline.gist: Whether a responsible father, mother or young person, every pilgrim sees themselves in one of them at the jamarat.

outline.heading: Shaytan only enters through your weaknesses
outline.gist: He has no power over you; like Umar, whose road Shaytan avoided, you stone the pride, fear and laziness he exploits.

outline.heading: The stoning is symbolic; human devils are worse
outline.gist: No need to rage at the pillar; it is a vow to stop submitting to him, and devils among humans are more dangerous.

outline.heading: The knife that would not cut and the great ransom
outline.gist: Isma'il turned his face away to spare his father; Ibrahim struck three times, then was told he had fulfilled the vision and given a ram.

outline.heading: Full submission without understanding
outline.gist: A command with no visible logic was obeyed because they trusted there must be a reason.

outline.heading: Eid: Allah never commands what harms you
outline.gist: He did not ask for all your wealth, only zakat; every command, liked or disliked, is in your interest, and the sacrifice is an annual reminder.

outline.heading: The House as a sanctuary
outline.gist: Ibrahim was shown the site to purify and rebuild; masajid are refuges from the brutality of the world.

outline.heading: Father and son rebuild the House
outline.gist: First spouses built a home, now a parent and child; Maqam Ibrahim is where he stood checking the dimensions.

outline.heading: The Black Stone from Paradise
outline.gist: When Isma'il, tired, returned, Jibril had already brought a stone from Abu Qubays that came from Paradise.

outline.heading: Their prayer: make us Muslims and show us our rites
outline.gist: They asked for acceptance, Muslim descendants and repentance; only one who fools himself turns from Ibrahim's way.

outline.heading: Tawaf in harmony with the universe
outline.gist: Circling shows respect and makes the House your centre; everything from atoms to galaxies rotates counterclockwise like the pilgrims.

outline.heading: The call to Hajj and Jibril's teaching at Arafah
outline.gist: Ibrahim proclaimed the pilgrimage and Jibril taught him the rites, asking whether he understood: another meaning of Arafah.

outline.heading: Ibrahim in the seventh heaven
outline.gist: He reclines against the heavenly House he mirrored with his effort, with children who died young, and sends greetings: Paradise is planted with dhikr.

quran.point: A person has only what he strove for: the meaning of sa'i.

Proclaim the Hajj and people will come on foot and on lean camels.
Ibrahim's way of submission passed to his sons.

hadith.gist: Hajar ran seven times between Safa and Marwa, heard a voice, and found the angel bringing forth Zamzam.
If the Hour comes while one of you holds a sapling, let him plant it.
May Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; had she left Zamzam alone it would have been a flowing spring.
If Umar takes a road, Shaytan takes another.
On the Night Journey the Prophet saw Ibrahim reclining against the Bayt al-Ma'mur in the seventh heaven, surrounded by children.
Ibrahim sent greetings to the ummah: Paradise has good soil and open land, and its plants are subhanAllah, alhamdulillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar.

2:67.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأۡمُرُكُمۡ أَن تَذۡبَحُواْ بَقَرَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُوࣰ اۖ قَالَ أَعُوذُ بِٱللَّهِ أَنۡ أَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
2:67.en: And when Moses said unto his people: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye sacrifice a cow, they said: Dost thou make game of us? He answered: Allah forbid that I should be among the foolish

2:68.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ لَّا فَارِضࣱ وَلَا بِكۡرٌ عَوَانُۢ بَيۡنَ ذَٰلِكَۖ فَٱفۡعَلُواْ مَا تُؤۡمَرُونَ
2:68.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us what (cow) she is. (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith, Verily she is a cow neither with calf nor immature; (she is) between the two conditions; so do that which ye are commanded

2:69.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوۡنُهَاۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ صَفۡرَآءُ فَاقِعࣱ لَّوۡنُهَا تَسُرُّ ٱلنَّٰظِرِينَ
2:69.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us of what colour she is. (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Verily she is a yellow cow. Bright is her colour, gladdening beholders

2:70.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ إِنَّ ٱلۡبَقَرَ تَشَٰبَهَ عَلَيۡنَا وَإِنَّآ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَمُهۡتَدُونَ
2:70.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us what (cow) she is. Lo! cows are much alike to us; and Lo! if Allah wills, we may be led aright

2:71.ar: قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ لَّا ذَلُولࣱ تُثِيرُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ وَلَا تَسۡقِي ٱلۡحَرۡثَ مُسَلَّمَةࣱ لَّا شِيَةَ فِيهَاۚ قَالُواْ ٱلۡـَٰٔنَ جِئۡتَ بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
2:71.en: (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Verily she is a cow unyoked; she plougheth not the soil nor watereth the tilth; whole and without mark. They said: Now thou bringest the truth. So they sacrificed her, though almost they did not

5:101.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَسۡـَٔلُواْ عَنۡ أَشۡيَآءَ إِن تُبۡدَ لَكُمۡ تَسُؤۡكُمۡ وَإِن تَسۡـَٔلُواْ عَنۡهَا حِينَ يُنَزَّلُ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ تُبۡدَ لَكُمۡ عَفَا ٱللَّهُ عَنۡهَاۗ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورٌ حَلِيمࣱ‏
5:101.en: O ye who believe! Ask not of things which, if they were made unto you, would trouble you; but if ye ask of them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made known unto you. Allah pardoneth this, for Allah is Forgiving, Clement
